claim: GGN is a unique giant GABAergic neuron that plays a central role in structuring olfactory codes in the locust mushroom body.
source: GGN, a unique giant GABAergic neuron that plays a central role in structuring olfactory codes in the locust mushroom body
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental work and modeling presented throughout the manuscript

claim: Depolarizing GGN at its input branch can globally inhibit KCs several hundred microns away.
source: Our simulations suggest that depolarizing GGN at its input branch can globally inhibit KCs several hundred microns away.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 2 demonstrating signal propagation through GGN's morphology

claim: GGN responds to odors with complex temporal patterns of depolarization and hyperpolarization that can vary with odors and across animals.
source: Our in vivo recordings show that GGN responds to odors with complex temporal patterns of depolarization and hyperpolarization that can vary with odors and across animals
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4

claim: Multiple types of olfactory receptor neurons can respond to a given odor with vigorous bursts of action potentials.
source: Multiple types of olfactory receptor neurons can respond to a given odor with vigorous bursts of action potentials
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994b; Friedrich and Laurent, 2001; Perez-Orive et al., 2002)

claim: Neurons in the pyriform cortex (vertebrates) or mushroom body (insects) respond to odors with only a spike or two.
source: while neurons deeper in the brain, in the pyriform cortex (vertebrates) or mushroom body (insects), respond to the same odor with only a spike or two
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994b; Friedrich and Laurent, 2001; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Cang and Isaacson, 2003; Bathellier et al., 2008; Poo and Isaacson, 2009)

claim: Information about odors in higher order neurons is represented sparsely by the identities of active neurons (population coding) and in the timing of the few spikes (temporal coding).
source: In these higher order neurons, information about odors is represented sparsely by the identities of the active neurons (population coding) and in the timing of the few spikes elicited in those neurons (temporal coding)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Stettler and Axel, 2009; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014)

claim: GABAergic neurons make important inhibitory contributions to olfactory transformations in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates multiple mechanisms interact to mediate these transformations, including important inhibitory contributions from GABAergic neurons
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Luna and Pettit, 2010; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014; Palmer and Harvey, 2014; Large et al., 2016; Large et al., 2018)

claim: In the absence of environmental odors, olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) in the locust antenna are spontaneously active.
source: In the absence of environmental odors, olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) in the antenna are spontaneously active.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the locust olfactory system

claim: Spontaneous activity in ORNs drives background spiking in PNs.
source: Spontaneous activity in ORNs drives background spiking in PNs (Joseph et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Joseph et al., 2012

claim: Spikes in PNs are coaxed into rhythmic waves by fast reciprocal interactions between excitatory PNs and inhibitory LNs.
source: Spikes in PNs are also coaxed into rhythmic waves by fast reciprocal interactions between excitatory PNs and inhibitory LNs
evidence: This is supported by citations (MacLeod and Laurent, 1996; Bazhenov et al., 2001)

claim: Kenyon cells (KCs) are nearly silent at rest and respond very selectively to odors by generating very few spikes.
source: Unlike the volubly spiking PNs, KCs are nearly silent at rest and respond very selectively to odors by generating very few spikes
evidence: This is supported by citations (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994b; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Joseph et al., 2012)

claim: Any given odor evokes responses in a small fraction of the KC population.
source: Thus, any given odor evokes responses in a small fraction of the KC population
evidence: This is supported by citations (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Stopfer et al., 2003)

claim: Sparseness of activity in KCs arises mainly from specialized membrane conductances that amplify only strong, synchronized input and a feedback circuit that tamps down their spiking with cyclic inhibition.
source: This sparseness of activity in KCs is thought to arise mainly from two factors: specialized membrane conductances that amplify only strong, synchronized input; and a feedback circuit that tamps down their spiking with cyclic inhibition
evidence: This is supported by citations (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Demmer and Kloppenburg, 2009; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014)

claim: In the locust, the main sources of inhibition to KCs are the giant GABAergic neurons (GGNs), one on each side of the brain.
source: In the locust the main sources of this inhibition are the giant GABAergic neurons (GGNs), one on each side of the brain
evidence: This is supported by citations (Leitch and Laurent, 1996; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Gupta and Stopfer, 2012)

claim: GGN receives excitatory input from all 50,000 KCs at synapses within the mushroom body's α lobe.
source: It is reported to receive excitatory input from all 50,000 KCs at synapses within the mushroom body's α lobe
evidence: This is stated based on prior reports

claim: GGN provides inhibitory feedback to all KCs 400–500 μm away within the calyx.
source: and, in turn, provide inhibitory feedback to all KCs 400–500 μm away within the calyx
evidence: This is stated based on prior reports

claim: GGN receives inhibitory input from a spiking neuron named 'Inhibitor of GGN' (IG) which itself receives inhibition from GGN.
source: In addition, GGN receives inhibitory input from a spiking neuron aptly named 'Inhibitor of GGN' (IG) which itself receives inhibition from GGN
evidence: This is stated in text and shown in Figure 1a (right), supported by citation (Papadopoulou et al., 2011)

claim: GGN is a non-spiking interneuron.
source: GGN is a non-spiking interneuron.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Leitch and Laurent, 1996; Papadopoulou et al., 2011) and the authors' own observations

claim: Odor presentations, spiking in KCs, and intracellular current injections depolarize GGN but do not cause it to generate spikes.
source: Odor presentations, spiking in KCs, and intracellular current injections have all been shown to depolarize GGN, but none of these stimuli causes GGN to generate spikes
evidence: This is supported by citations (Leitch and Laurent, 1996; Papadopoulou et al., 2011) and the authors' own observations

claim: 2–5 mV depolarizations in nonspiking interneurons suffice to evoke changes in the membrane potentials of their post-synaptic neurons.
source: Prior studies in invertebrates have shown that 2–5 mV depolarizations in nonspiking interneurons suffice to evoke changes in the membrane potentials of their post-synaptic neurons
evidence: This is supported by citations (Burrows and Siegler, 1978; Manor et al., 1997)

claim: Signals arising in GGN's α lobe branches remain strong enough to provide global inhibition to KCs in the calyx.
source: Our model showed that, although electrical signals do undergo substantial attenuation as they travel through GGN, signals arising in its α lobe branches appear to remain strong enough to provide global inhibition to KCs in the calyx.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2

claim: Synaptic connection strengths onto KCs must be heterogeneous to generate the types of membrane potential patterns observed in GGN.
source: First, to generate the types of membrane potential patterns we observed in GGN, the synaptic connection strengths onto KCs must be heterogeneous.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5

claim: GGN's periods of hyperpolarization could not be explained by disinhibition of IG from GGN.
source: Although GGN receives reciprocal feedback from IG (Papadopoulou et al., 2011), the periods of hyperpolarization could not be explained by disinhibition of IG from GGN.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling and in vivo recordings shown in Figures 8 and 9

claim: IG receives direct excitation from another, presently unknown odor-activated pathway in addition to receiving input from GGN.
source: Instead, our model predicts that this behavior could arise if, in addition to receiving input from GGN, IG also receives direct excitation from another, presently unknown odor-activated pathway.
evidence: This is a prediction based on computational modeling and in vivo recordings shown in Figures 8 and 9

claim: A small portion of KCs spike at relatively high rates.
source: Additionally, our model replicated emergent features of the olfactory network not explicitly programmed into it, such as the appearance of a small portion of KCs spiking at relatively high rates.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figures 6 and 7, and in vivo recordings

claim: GGN has a reliable and unique location and morphology.
source: As previously shown, GGN has a reliable and unique location and morphology
evidence: This is supported by citations (Weiss, 1978; Leitch and Laurent, 1996; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Gupta and Stopfer, 2012)

claim: On each side of the brain, GGN's soma is located ventrally, just anterior to the optic nerve.
source: On each side of the brain, its soma is located ventrally, just anterior to the optic nerve.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on observations

claim: A single neurite emerges from GGN's soma, travels toward the posterior and dorsal side of the brain, and splits into two branches, one innervating the α lobe and the other the mushroom body.
source: A single neurite emerges from GGN's soma, travels toward the posterior and dorsal side of the brain, and splits there into two branches, one innervating the α lobe and the other the mushroom body.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on observations shown in Figure 1

claim: Myriad thin fibers emerge from the stems of GGN's calyceal branches, splitting into very fine feather-like neurites that wrap densely around the peduncle.
source: We further observed, for the first time, myriad thin fibers that emerge from the stems of the calyceal branches, splitting into very fine feather-like neurites that wrap densely around the peduncle, with some investing the peduncle core
evidence: This is a novel morphological observation shown in Figure 1b

claim: The neurites in GGN's calyx and lateral horn are dotted with many irregular bouton-like structures.
source: The neurites in the calyx and lateral horn are dotted with many irregular bouton-like structures
evidence: This is a morphological observation shown in Figure 1c

claim: The branches in GGN's α lobe are relatively smooth.
source: whereas the branches in α lobe are relatively smooth
evidence: This is a morphological observation shown in Figure 1d

claim: The maximum path length of GGN's neuronal trees is on the order of 2 mm.
source: Analyzing these traces, we found that the maximum path length of the neuronal trees (i.e., the maximum distance between any two points on the neuronal tree when traversed along the neurites) was on the order of 2 mm
evidence: This is based on analysis of morphological traces

claim: The maximum physical length of GGN is on the order of 1 mm.
source: and the maximum physical length (i.e., Euclidean distance between any two points on the neuron in three-dimensions) was on the order of 1 mm
evidence: This is based on analysis of morphological traces

claim: Some neurites of GGN at their thickest are nearly 20 μm in diameter.
source: Some neurites at their thickest were nearly 20 μm in diameter.
evidence: This is based on analysis of morphological traces

claim: The total traced branch length of GGN is about 65 mm.
source: The total traced branch length (i.e., the sum of the lengths of all the neurites) was about 65 mm
evidence: This is based on analysis of morphological traces

claim: GGN falls into the 99.75th percentile for total branch length compared to 96,831 vertebrate and invertebrate neurons cataloged in the neuromorpho.org database.
source: Compared to 96,831 vertebrate and invertebrate neurons cataloged in the neuromorpho.org database, GGN fell into the 99.75th percentile for total branch length
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis with the neuromorpho.org database

claim: GGN falls into the 99.95th percentile for number of branch points compared to 96,831 vertebrate and invertebrate neurons cataloged in the neuromorpho.org database.
source: and the 99.95th percentile for number of branch points
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis with the neuromorpho.org database

claim: Strong odor stimuli depolarize GGN by about 10 mV in recordings made near the base of the α lobe branch.
source: Because strong odor stimuli depolarize GGN by about 10 mV in recordings made near the base of the α lobe branch
evidence: This is supported by citation (Papadopoulou et al., 2011) and the authors' own observations shown in Figure 4

claim: A 10 mV depolarization in GGN's α lobe branch yields depolarizations ranging from ~5–9 mV throughout the calyx.
source: we first stepped the clamp voltage in the α lobe branch to −40 mV, and, after holding it there for 450 ms, measured the resulting depolarizations throughout the model GGN (Figure 2a inset). Notably, the extent of signal attenuation was substantial and varied throughout the calyx, yielding depolarizations ranging from ~5–9 mV.
evidence: This is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 2

claim: The signal in GGN decreases with branch distance from the α lobe, leaving the least amount of signal at the medial portion of the lateral calyceal branch.
source: The signal decreased with branch distance from the α lobe, leaving the least amount of signal at the medial portion of the lateral calyceal branch
evidence: This is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 2b,c and Figure 2—video 1

claim: Except for extreme values of membrane and cytoplasmic resistivity, signals from GGN's α lobe remain strong enough throughout the calyx (>2–5 mV) to support synaptic transmission.
source: This analysis suggests that signal transmission in GGN is robust: except for the most extreme values of this parameter range, signals from the α lobe remained strong enough throughout the calyx (>2–5 mV) to support synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is based on computational simulations exploring parameter ranges shown in Figure 2g

claim: Feedback inhibition from GGN expands the dynamic range of KCs.
source: These results suggested that feedback inhibition from GGN allows an individual KC to function effectively over a larger dynamic range of inputs.
evidence: This is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3

claim: Feedback inhibition from GGN increases the KC spiking threshold.
source: As expected, baseline inhibition from spontaneous activity in GGN increased the KC's threshold for spiking.
evidence: This is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3

claim: The GGN-coupled KC continues to spike over a much larger range of current injection than an isolated KC, which quickly saturates.
source: Notably, though, the GGN-coupled KC continued to spike over a much larger range of current injection than the isolated KC, which quickly saturated to a level where it could no longer spike
evidence: This is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3b,c

claim: Almost a quarter of the odor-GGN pairs in in vivo recordings showed reliable hyperpolarizations at some point in the odor response (40 out of 169).
source: Almost a quarter of the odor-GGN pairs in our in vivo recordings showed reliable hyperpolarizations at some point in the odor response (40 out of 169).
evidence: This is based on in vivo electrophysiological recordings

claim: Sustained GGN responses require heterogeneous input to KCs.
source: Sustained GGN responses require heterogeneous input to KCs
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5

claim: 77% of PNs have a spontaneous firing rate of 2.6 spikes/s.
source: Thus, 77% of the PN spike trains were assigned a spontaneous firing rate of 2.6 spikes/s
evidence: This is based on statistics from prior studies (Mazor and Laurent, 2005; Jortner et al., 2007)

claim: During odor stimulation, 20% of spontaneously active PNs switch to 20 spikes/s modulated by 20 Hz oscillations.
source: during odor stimulation, 20% of these PNs were switched to 20 spikes/s modulated by the 20 Hz oscillations generated in the antennal lobe
evidence: This is based on statistics from prior studies (Mazor and Laurent, 2005; Jortner et al., 2007)

claim: During odor stimulation, 10% of spontaneously active PNs are inhibited (no spikes).
source: and 10% were inhibited (no spikes)
evidence: This is based on statistics from prior studies (Mazor and Laurent, 2005; Jortner et al., 2007)

claim: Synaptic strengths follow a lognormal distribution.
source: Synaptic strengths follow a lognormal distribution
evidence: This is supported by citations (Song et al., 2005; Loewenstein et al., 2011; Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014)

claim: A model combining heterogeneous connectivity with structured PN firing patterns gives rise to GGN voltage traces with sustained depolarization and temporal dynamics characteristic of responses observed in vivo.
source: However, a model combining heterogeneous connectivity with structured PN firing patterns gave rise to GGN voltage traces that included sustained depolarization and temporal dynamics more characteristic of responses we had observed in vivo
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5h,i

claim: While most KCs produce 0–2 odor-elicited spikes, a few KCs spike much more.
source: The distribution of firing rates of the KC population in our simulations showed that, while most KCs produced 0–2 odor-elicited spikes, a few KCs spiked much more
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The average spontaneous firing rate of KCs is very low (~0.09 Hz).
source: On average, the spontaneous firing rates of these real KCs were very low (~0.09 Hz)
evidence: This is based on patch clamp recordings from 147 KCs in 114 animals

claim: KC firing rates reach only somewhat higher rates during odor presentation (~0.15 Hz) and immediately after odor termination (~0.16 Hz).
source: and reached only somewhat higher rates during odor presentation and immediately after odor termination (~0.15 and~0.16 Hz, respectively, Figure 6b)
evidence: This is based on patch clamp recordings from 147 KCs in 114 animals, shown in Figure 6b

claim: The distribution of spike counts in KCs tested in vivo is clustered close to 0 but includes a long rightward tail.
source: Overall, the distribution of spike counts in KCs we tested in vivo was clustered close to 0 but included a long rightward tail
evidence: This is based on in vivo recordings shown in Figure 6g

claim: High spike-rate KCs in the model are not a static population, but rather change in identity, reflecting emergent features of the network.
source: first, the high spike-rate KCs in our model are not a static population, but rather change in identity, reflecting emergent features of the network's distribution of synaptic conductances, PN input, and GGN feedback
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 7

claim: High-spike rate KCs augment the depolarization of GGN to realistic levels.
source: and second, high-spike rate KCs augment the depolarization of GGN to realistic levels.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 7

claim: Odor presentations cause the frequency of IPSPs in GGN to increase.
source: Our recordings made in vivo from GGN revealed IPSPs in the absence of odors, and that odor presentations caused the frequency of IPSPs to increase (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 198 pairs, W = 2328.5, p<<0.001
evidence: This is based on in vivo recordings shown in Figure 8, with statistical analysis

claim: IG's firing rate begins to increase before GGN's membrane potential returns to baseline.
source: Notably, as evident in Figure 8b, IG's firing rate begins to increase before GGN's membrane potential returns to baseline.
evidence: This is based on in vivo recordings shown in Figure 8b

claim: IG's odor response cannot be driven solely by a reduction in inhibition from GGN.
source: This result rules out the possibility that IG's odor response is driven solely by a reduction in inhibition from GGN
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that IG begins to spike before GGN's membrane potential returns to baseline

claim: IG receives odor-driven excitation from another pathway.
source: and suggests, rather, that IG receives odor-driven excitation from another pathway
evidence: This is an inference based on in vivo recordings and computational modeling

claim: Realistic hyperpolarization in GGN's membrane potential can be reproduced by adding excitatory synapses to IG from either the KCs or the PNs.
source: Using our model, we could indeed reproduce realistic hyperpolarization in GGN's membrane potential by adding excitatory synapses to IG from either the KCs or the PNs
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 9a–e

claim: Odor-specific patterns of spiking across the PN population may underlie the variability in GGN hyperpolarizations elicited by different odors.
source: Our simulations suggest that odor-specific patterns of spiking across the PN population (Stopfer et al., 2003) may underlie this variability
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 9b–i

claim: Spontaneous IPSPs in GGN persist in preparations with silenced PNs and KCs.
source: We found that spontaneous IPSPs in GGN persisted in preparations with silenced PNs and KCs
evidence: This is based on in vivo recordings shown in Figure 9j

claim: IG's spontaneous spiking either arises intrinsically or is driven by a source other than PNs or KCs.
source: demonstrating that IG's spontaneous spiking either arises intrinsically or is driven by a source other than PNs or KCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on in vivo recordings showing spontaneous IPSPs persist when PNs and KCs are silenced

claim: GGN has the biophysical capacity to convey signals from KCs at GGN's α lobe branches to the calyx, providing effective global inhibition to all KCs.
source: Thus, we conclude that GGN has the biophysical capacity to convey signals from KCs at GGN's α lobe branches to the calyx, providing effective global inhibition to all KCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on computational modeling and comparison with prior studies on non-spiking neurons

claim: Depolarizations of only about 2 mV in a non-spiking interneuron in the locust metathoracic ganglion can change the firing rate of its postsynaptic motor neuron.
source: For example, (Burrows and Siegler, 1978) showed that depolarizations of only about 2 mV in a non-spiking interneuron in the metathoracic ganglion of the locust can change the firing rate of its postsynaptic motor neuron.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burrows and Siegler, 1978

claim: In a graded synapse in the lobster stomatogastric ganglion, voltage steps from −50 mV to −45 mV can reliably evoke postsynaptic effects.
source: Similarly, (Manor et al., 1997) showed in a graded synapse in the lobster stomatogastric ganglion that voltage steps from −50 mV to −45 mV can reliably evoke postsynaptic effects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manor et al., 1997

claim: Imaging experiments in APL revealed different levels of Ca2+ activity in different spatial regions of its arbor when the animal was stimulated with low concentrations of odors.
source: Consistent with this, imaging experiments in APL, the Drosophila analog of GGN (Lin et al., 2014) revealed different levels of Ca2+ activity in different spatial regions of its arbor when the animal was stimulated with low concentrations of odors (Inada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inada et al., 2017

claim: Some KCs are more effective than others at activating APL.
source: Inada et al. also found that some KCs are more effective than others at activating APL
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inada et al., 2017

claim: APL provides diverse levels of inhibition to different subsets of KCs in the same brain.
source: and that APL, in turn, provides diverse levels of inhibition to different subsets of KCs in the same brain
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inada et al., 2017

claim: APL can provide local inhibition to a subset of KCs, likely through dendrodendritic connections between KCs and APL within the calyx.
source: By optogenetically activating a small subset of PNs, Inada et al. showed that APL could provide local inhibition to a subset of KCs, likely through dendrodendritic connections between KCs and APL within the calyx.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inada et al., 2017

claim: APL receives synaptic connections from KCs throughout its arbor, including within the calyx.
source: Indeed, reconstructions of APL based on serial section electron microscope images show that it receives synaptic connections from KCs throughout its arbor, including within the calyx (Eichler et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eichler et al., 2017 and Zheng et al., 2018

claim: Strong odor stimuli drive both GGN and APL to provide global inhibition to all KCs.
source: In vivo, strong odor stimuli appear to drive both GGN and APL to provide global inhibition to all KCs
evidence: This is supported by citations (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014)

claim: Feedback inhibition from GGN sparsens the firing of KCs and imposes rhythmic time windows on their responses.
source: Inhibition from GGN is known to sparsen the firing of KCs and to impose rhythmic time windows on their responses
evidence: This is supported by citations (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Gupta and Stopfer, 2012)

claim: Large-scale feedforward inhibition expands the dynamic range of cortical neurons.
source: Large-scale feedforward inhibition has previously been shown to expand the dynamic range of cortical neurons (Pouille et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pouille et al., 2009

claim: In Drosophila, feedback inhibition from APL expands the dynamic range of KCs.
source: and in Drosophila, feedback inhibition from APL, the analog of GGN, expands the dynamic range of KCs (Inada et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inada et al., 2017

claim: Blocking inhibitory inputs to KCs in Drosophila narrowed the dynamic range of their odor responses.
source: This prediction is consistent with observations made by imaging calcium in Drosophila where blocking inhibitory inputs to KCs narrowed the dynamic range of their odor responses (Inada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inada et al., 2017

claim: Spikes in IG correlate one-to-one with IPSPs in GGN.
source: However, a previous report showed spikes in IG correlate one-to-one with IPSPs in GGN (Papadopoulou et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Papadopoulou et al., 2011

claim: It has been hypothesized that IG receives input from KCs.
source: It has been hypothesized that IG receives input from KCs (Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Papadopoulou et al., 2011

claim: Different classes of KCs differentially activate APL in Drosophila.
source: Different classes of KCs have been reported to differentially activate APL in Drosophila (Inada et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inada et al., 2017

claim: GGN's membrane potential rests at about −51 mV in vivo.
source: In vivo, intracellular recordings (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; and our own) show GGN's membrane potential rests at about −51 mV.
evidence: This is supported by citation (Papadopoulou et al., 2011) and the authors' own observations

claim: Each KC receives input from 50% of the PN population.
source: Half of the PN population was randomly and independently selected as presynaptic partners for each KC.
evidence: This is based on prior observations (Jortner et al., 2007) and implemented in the model

claim: Any two KCs share about 50% of their presynaptic PNs.
source: Thus, with 800 PNs and each KC receiving input from 400 PNs, the expected number of PNs shared by any two KCs is 400 * 400/800 = 200, that is they share about 50% of their presynaptic PNs, as shown in vivo (Jortner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on mathematical calculation and supported by citation to Jortner et al., 2007

claim: KCs require strong and coincident input from PNs to spike.
source: Indeed, a version of our model in which all KCs synapse upon IG reliably reproduced fairly realistic odor-elicited hyperpolarizations in GGN. This result leads us to hypothesize that KCs, which require strong and coincident input from PNs to spike (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Jortner et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Jortner et al., 2007)

claim: The model GGN was segmented into 5283 isopotential compartments.
source: To account for branches and changes in the diameters of processes that affect electrotonic distance, we segmented the model GGN into 5283 isopotential compartments.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model implementation

claim: The membrane resistivity in the GGN model was set to 33 kΩ-cm2.
source: We set the membrane resistivity in the model to 33 kΩ-cm2 following published descriptions obtained from other non-spiking neurons in the locust (Laurent, 1991)
evidence: This is a model parameter based on citation to Laurent, 1991

claim: The specific membrane capacitance in the GGN model was set to 1 μF/cm2.
source: the specific membrane capacitance to 1 μF/cm2, the approximate value for cell membranes
evidence: This is a model parameter based on citations (Curtis and Cole, 1938; Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952; Gentet et al., 2000)

claim: The cytoplasmic resistivity in the GGN model was set to 100 Ω-cm.
source: and the cytoplasmic resistivity to 100 Ω-cm, a typical order-of-magnitude value for neurons
evidence: This is a model parameter based on citations (Hodgkin and Rushton, 1946; Stuart and Spruston, 1998; Roth and Häusser, 2001)
